title: What Vladimir Putin Really Thinks About Americans

levels.name: The File
beats: Hate would mean you counted as a person.
You are weather. A climate that repeats.
I have been waiting you out since you had a flip phone.
Weather is not an enemy. Weather is a calendar.
You know my name. I have known your type longer than you have had a passport.
The first American I ever met was not a person. It was a commercial.
White teeth. A red cup the size of a head.
A family hugging in a kitchen so bright it has to be fake, because it is.
That is not entertainment to me. That is your self-portrait, sold back to you at scale.
You talk in restaurants like the room is empty.
You ask a stranger their job before their name.
You wear the logo on purpose.
In the classroom they still draw you with a flag on the sleeve and no idea where Kaliningrad is.
That drawing is not an insult. It is an operating assumption.
I log the smile.
You smile at cameras, at cashiers, at people who have not earned it.
In my notes a smile is a tell: you want to be liked more than you want to win.
I watch your movies the way a surgeon watches an X-ray.
The hero who breaks the rules and is rewarded. The president who is secretly good.
The war that ends in a speech.
I do not believe the movies. I believe that you do.
By the time you walk into a real room, the cartoon is already sitting in the other chair.
You will spend the first twenty minutes fighting a drawing of yourself.
Most of you never notice.
The second folder is thinner, and it cost more to build.
It is not about what you say. It is about what you buy.
You will sell a principle for a cheaper flight.
You will sell a friendship for a better rate.
You will sell a secret, I am certain, for a feeling: being the smartest man at a table of people who already know.
Money is the lazy tool. I do not lead with money.
I lead with access.
A conference in Vienna. A think-tank panel.
A private dinner where someone important remembered your paper.
Ego is cheaper than cash, and it does not show up on a bank statement.
You think of yourself as a citizen. I think of you as a market.
Markets have seasons. Markets punish hesitation.
Markets, above all, come back after they crash and ask for the same product with a new slogan.
That is the most useful sentence I have on you.
You come back.
I respect the hardware. I will tell you that in private, and I am not lying.
Carriers. Satellites. A budget that looks like a hallucination when you write it in rubles.
I do not respect the will.
That is the split. Everything after it hangs on that split.
I counted the years in Afghanistan. I counted the years in Iraq.
I counted how long a democracy argues with itself before the arguing becomes the mission.
I have a number for that. I have tested it.
You will bomb a mountain. You will not occupy a winter.
You will announce a red line, and then hold a hearing about the announcement.
I do not need you weak. I need you busy.
A superpower with three crises and a midterm is, to me, a superpower with no crises at all.
The soldier in my folder is not a coward.
He is a man whose country will bring him home the moment the pictures get bad.
I plan around the pictures. I plan around the fact that you have evening news.
This is the page I underline.
You replace the entire foreign policy of a nuclear state the way other countries replace a cabinet minister.
On a Tuesday. With a parade.
A treaty is not a treaty. It is a mood. A mood that expires in January.
I do not take your word. I take your calendar.
How many months until your election. How many months until the other party's primary.
How many months until the man who shook my hand is explaining himself to a committee.
You think consistency is a virtue.
I think consistency is a problem I do not have to have with you.
The useful move is not to convince you.
It is to wait until you convince yourselves of the opposite of whatever you said last year.
You are very good at that. You call it a mandate.
Somewhere in a room with bad heating, a date gets written next to a name.
The date is Inauguration Day. The name is whoever you just elected.
The folder does not change. Only the heading does.
I do not need to invent your arguments. You publish them. You fund them.
You put them on the internet with a donate button.
A university panel about your own decline.
A journalist who hates the Pentagon more than he hates the tanks.
A celebrity reading a statement about a war they could not find on a map an hour ago.
The choir is not secret. The choir has a mailing list.
In the old building we used to plant stories. Now we retweet.
The skill is the same: find the American already angry at America, and give him a bigger room.
You call this a marketplace of ideas. I call it a buffet.
I do not have to be the chef. I only have to be hungry at the right hour.
The most valuable American in the folder is not a spy. It is a sincere person.
Sincere people do not need to be recruited. They need to be amplified.
They will do the rest on their own time, in their own voice, at no cost to my budget.
If you are waiting for a villain in a dark coat to hand someone an envelope, you have misunderstood the century.
The envelope is a quote. The quote is yours.
The Americans I actually drink with are not the cartoon.
They are the ones in Mayfair. In Geneva.
On a yacht registered nowhere and docked everywhere.
They speak quietly. They know where the money sits when it is tired of flags.
They will lecture a camera about democracy at lunch.
And ask at dinner whether the sanction list has a loophole with a name on it.
This is the most dangerous page, because it is the most intimate.
It says you are not a people. You are two countries sharing a language.
One of them votes. One of them invoices.
I have watched a senator's son sit at a table his father could not be seen at.
I do not moralize about it. Moralizing is your hobby.
This American is not a hypocrite. Hypocrisy would require a standard.
This American is a professional. Professionals can be scheduled.
The cartoon is for television. This one is for the work.
I have a cleaner word for your politics than you do. I call it a machine.
Machines have tolerances. Machines jam.
Machines, if you study them long enough, make the same noise before they fail.
Fifty percent plus one. That is the whole religion.
Not truth. Not competence.
Fifty percent plus one, and then four years of the winner pretending the loser was never real.
I do not need to pick your president. I need to pick your argument.
An argument that lasts from August to November is a strategic pause I did not have to pay for.
You think I want you divided. That is too flattering.
Division is a side effect.
What I want is your attention spent inward. On each other. On a clip.
On a man in a supermarket who said the wrong thing into a phone.
A country staring at itself cannot stare at a border.
I have measured this. I will keep measuring it.
Every time your news cycle eats a week, someone else's map gets a new road.
The machine is not evil in the folder. Evil is a movie word.
The machine is predictable.
Predictable is the highest compliment I give an enemy.
A new American walks onto a stage and talks about reset. About strength.
About a line that will not be crossed this time.
I do not cheer. I do not panic. I open the same folder.
The cartoon is still in it. The price tag. The soldier who goes home.
The headings have not moved in thirty years. Only the photographs have.
I do not need you to be worse. I need you to be you.
Loud. Rich. Impatient.
Convinced that history is a sequel in which you still have the best effects budget.
You will ask, at the end of a video like this, whether I am right.
That question is also in the folder. Americans love a verdict.
You love to put yourselves on the scale and argue with the reading.
The folder does not care about the verdict.
It cares that you watched. That you felt seen, or insulted.
And that tomorrow you will argue about it with each other instead of looking up.
Someone new is already writing a speech about how this time will be different.
In the room with the bad heating, I sharpen a pencil.
The cycle does not continue because I am brilliant.
It continues because you are familiar.
